The town that refused to let its lido die

Eight years after the council shut its art deco pool, Ashby Marsh lido is open, packed and paying its way. How a town of 14,000 raised the money, fixed the leaks, and learned to run a swimming pool — and the unlikely neighbour that might keep it warm.

By Folasade Ogunleye · Photographs by Tam Brodie · Published 7 November 2025, 06:00 · Updated 7 November 2025, 11:20 · 18 min read

Share Email 214 comments

At 6.30 on a September morning, the queue outside Ashby Marsh lido stretches past the bus shelter and halfway to the war memorial. There are retired teachers in dryrobes, a man with a tattoo of a seahorse, two teenagers who have been coming every day since July for a bet, and a woman called Margaret Ennis, who is 87 and has a lane she considers her own.

“I learned to swim here in 1946,” she tells me, while stretching against the railings in a way that makes my back hurt to watch. “My father held me up by the costume straps. When they closed it, I cried in the car park. I don't cry. I didn't cry at my wedding.”

When the gates open, the queue funnels past a volunteer with a clipboard and a cash tin that nobody uses any more, through changing rooms that smell of new paint and old chlorine, and out into the light. The pool is 50 metres long, painted a blue that the restoration team spent three months arguing about, with a stepped white fountain at the far end that was restored by a stonemason from the next valley who once worked on a cathedral. The water this morning is 21 degrees. The air is 11. Steam drifts off the surface. Margaret is in first.

For seven years, between 2016 and 2023, none of this happened. This is the story of how a small town, written off by its own council and told by experts that the pool was beyond saving, raised the money, fixed it, and worked out how to run it — and of the slightly odd plan, involving cheese and milk, that might keep it open into the autumn.

“Beyond economic repair”

Ashby Marsh lido opened in June 1937, one of more than 150 outdoor pools built in Britain between the wars, when open-air swimming was promoted as a cure for everything from rickets to moral decline. The town paid for it with a loan from central government and a penny on the rates, and the opening ceremony was attended by an Olympic diver who, the local paper reported, “performed a swallow dive of breathtaking grace, despite the cold”.

For most of the 20th century it was the centre of summer in Ashby Marsh. Older residents remember diving boards (removed in 1989 for safety reasons), a café that sold tea and Bovril, swimming galas with brass bands, and courting couples on the terraces. By the 2000s, though, it was struggling. Visitor numbers had fallen, the 1960s plant room was failing, and the pool lost so much water through cracks in its concrete shell that the council's own engineers estimated it was leaking the equivalent of a full domestic bath every four minutes.

In 2015, a structural survey commissioned by the district council concluded that the pool tank needed a new lining, the filtration and pumping system needed replacing entirely, the changing rooms did not meet modern accessibility standards, and the fountain was “in a dangerous condition”. The estimated cost of the work was £1.9 million. The council, facing cuts to its budget of nearly a third over the previous five years, described the pool as “beyond economic repair” and voted to close it at the end of the 2016 season.

“I understood the decision, I really did,” says Councillor Rachel Hume, who was on the council's leisure committee at the time and voted for closure. “We were closing libraries. We were cutting care budgets. I couldn't look a family who'd lost their mum's home care in the eye and say we'd spent nearly two million on a swimming pool that's open four months a year.” She pauses. “I was also wrong about whether the town would let it go. I underestimated them completely.”

A meeting in the scout hut

The Friends of Ashby Marsh Lido was founded at a public meeting in the scout hut in February 2017. Organisers expected thirty people. More than three hundred turned up, and the overflow stood outside in the rain listening through an open window.

The group's first chair was Dev Kalsi, a quantity surveyor who had moved to the town five years earlier and had never swum in the pool. “I went to the meeting because my daughter wanted to go,” he says. “I came out as chair. I'm still not entirely sure how.”

Kalsi's professional background turned out to be crucial. He went through the council's £1.9 million estimate line by line and concluded that some of it could be done more cheaply, some could be phased, and some could be done by volunteers. “The survey was correct about what was wrong,” he says. “But it priced everything as if a big contractor would do it all at once, to the highest specification. That's how councils have to price things. It's not how a community has to do things.”

His revised plan came in at £1.32 million, split into two phases. Phase one — the essential repairs to reopen — was the new pool lining, new filtration and pumps, and the accessible changing rooms. Phase two — the fountain, the café and the terraces — could wait.

The next problem was who would own the pool. The council was willing to transfer the lido to a community group on a 99-year lease for a nominal rent of £1 a year, but only if the group could show it had the money for phase one and a realistic plan to cover running costs. In 2018, the Friends became a community benefit society, a type of organisation owned by its members and run for the benefit of the community, which can raise money by selling shares to the public.

“The survey was correct about what was wrong. But it priced everything as if a big contractor would do it all at once.” — Dev Kalsi

The money

The fundraising took four years, and was, by everyone's account, exhausting.

The largest single chunk came from community shares. In 2019, the society offered shares at £50 each, with a minimum investment of £100 and a maximum of £20,000. Shareholders get one vote each, whatever the size of their investment, and may receive a small amount of interest once the lido is making a surplus. The share offer raised £640,000 from just over 2,100 investors, most of them local, some of them former residents who had moved away decades ago and remembered the pool from their childhoods.

Then came the pandemic. The share offer had closed in February 2020, a month before the first lockdown, and for a while the whole project looked doomed. Grant funders froze their programmes. Building costs rose sharply. Kalsi's £1.32 million plan, re-costed in 2021, came back at £1.61 million.

The gap was closed by an online crowdfunding appeal launched in April 2021 under the slogan “Fill the pool”. The idea came from Leah Mortimer, then a 26-year-old graphic designer, who designed a cartoon of the pool that filled up, pixel by pixel, as donations came in. People could sponsor a tile (£25), a lane rope (£250) or a day of the season (£1,000), and every donor's name was promised a place on a board in the entrance. Over the eight weeks of the campaign, 5,300 people gave a total of £412,000, including a single anonymous donation of £30,000 that arrived, Mortimer remembers, at 3am on the last night.

“We'd been stuck at about 85% for a week,” she says. “Everyone was knackered. I'd stopped refreshing the page. Then my phone started buzzing at three in the morning and I thought someone had died. It was the pool filling up.”

The rest of the money came from grants — a heritage lottery grant of £350,000, smaller grants from a sports charity and two local trusts — and from a long list of smaller efforts: a sponsored swim across a reservoir, a cookbook of residents' recipes, a calendar featuring the (fully clothed, mostly) members of the men's walking football team, and a pub quiz that ran every month for four years and raised, by the Friends' count, £23,640.

Ashby Marsh lido in numbers

  • Opened: June 1937
  • Closed: September 2016
  • Reopened: 27 May 2023
  • Pool: 50m x 18m, unheated (for now)
  • Council estimate to repair (2015): £1.9m
  • Final cost of phase one: £1.58m
  • Community shares: £640,000 from 2,100+ investors
  • “Fill the pool” crowdfunder: £412,000 from 5,300 donors
  • Heritage lottery grant: £350,000
  • Visits in the 2025 season: 61,400

Building it

Work started in September 2021 and was supposed to take a year. It took twenty months.

The first surprise was underneath the pool. When contractors broke out the old concrete at the deep end, they found that the original 1937 builders had laid it directly onto a bed of clay that swells and shrinks with the seasons, which explained most of the cracks. The fix — a drainage layer and a reinforced slab — added four months and £140,000 to the bill, and was paid for by a second, smaller share offer and a loan from a social investment fund.

The second surprise was the volunteers. More than 400 people signed up to help, and while they could not do the specialist work, they did almost everything else: stripping paint from the railings, laying paving, building benches, planting the gardens around the terraces, sanding and varnishing the changing-room doors, and, memorably, removing an estimated 11 tonnes of rubbish, including a shopping trolley, two motorbikes and a wedding dress, from the dried-out pool in the first month.

“I still don't know who the wedding dress belonged to,” says Kalsi. “We put a notice up. Nobody came forward. I like to think it was a happy ending.”

Then there was the blue. The pool's original colour had been lost under decades of repainting, and the society's heritage group wanted to match the 1937 shade exactly. A conservation specialist took paint samples from a corner of the pool that had been covered by a later plant-room extension, and found eleven layers, the earliest a pale, slightly greenish blue. A vocal minority of members wanted something brighter and more “Mediterranean”. The argument ran for three months, across two members' meetings and a very long thread on the society's online forum, and was settled by a vote at which, according to the minutes, 312 members chose the original colour and 97 chose the brighter one. “Democracy,” says Kalsi, “is exhausting. But it's the right colour.”

The fountain at the far end — a stepped white cascade in the shape of a stylised wave, which had been fenced off since 2009 — was the last thing to be finished, even though it was technically part of phase two. A stonemason, Gethin Prowse, offered to restore it at cost after reading about the project. He spent most of the winter of 2022 on it, replacing crumbling sections with new cast stone made to match, and rebuilding the pump that sends water down its steps. On the opening day, when it was switched on for the first time in fourteen years, people applauded. Prowse, by several accounts, had to go and sit in his van for a while.

The final bill for phase one came to £1.58 million, slightly under the re-costed estimate, mostly thanks to the volunteers and a contractor who, in Kalsi's words, “got emotionally involved and stopped charging us for half the things he should have”.

The lido finally reopened on 27 May 2023. Margaret Ennis was the first person in the water, by unanimous agreement. A brass band played. It rained.

Learning to run a pool

Raising the money, it turned out, was the easy part. Running a 50-metre outdoor pool is a business with high fixed costs, a short season and a product that depends entirely on the weather.

The lido employs eleven permanent staff, including a general manager, Helen Strachan, who previously ran a leisure centre in the city, and up to 40 seasonal lifeguards and café workers in the summer. Every session needs a minimum number of qualified lifeguards on the poolside by law, whether there are ten swimmers or six hundred. Chemicals, water testing, insurance and electricity for the pumps cost tens of thousands of pounds a year before anyone gets wet.

The first season, 2023, lost money: about £62,000, according to the society's published accounts. A cold, wet June cut attendances by more than a third, and the café, run by volunteers, was chaotic. “We had people who'd baked cakes at home for the café, which was lovely, but we had no idea what we were selling or what it cost us,” says Strachan. “We had a till that didn't work and an honesty box that was, let's say, optimistic.”

For 2024, Strachan made a series of unglamorous changes. The café was brought in-house with a paid manager and a short menu. Early-morning and evening sessions were extended, because those turned out to be when the most committed swimmers came. Pre-booking was introduced for the busiest sessions, which cut queues and made staffing easier to plan. Prices were reviewed, with a concession rate for people on low incomes, free swimming for children under five, and season tickets for regulars. The 2024 and 2025 season tickets — £45 for the whole season for members of the society — sold out within days, and there is now a waiting list.

The 2024 season broke even. The 2025 season, helped by a long, hot summer, made a surplus of about £48,000, which the society has put into a reserve for repairs. Attendance reached 61,400 visits, more than in any year since the 1970s.

Strachan is wary of drawing too many conclusions from one good summer. “We're a weather business,” she says. “We had a fantastic year, but the next one could be like 2023. The reserve is there so that a bad summer doesn't mean we close again.”

More than a pool

Ask anyone at the lido what it means to the town, and you get the same word again and again: “together”.

It is used by schools, which bring classes in for swimming lessons during the summer term. It is used by a club for people living with dementia, whose members swim, or sit by the pool, on Tuesday mornings with their carers. There's a women-only evening session, a session for people with disabilities, with a pool hoist that the Friends fundraised for separately, and a Friday-night “lido late” with music and the café open until ten.

Dr Owen Penhaligon, a GP at the town's health centre, has started “prescribing” the lido — not formally, but as part of the social prescribing scheme that links patients with local activities. “I've had patients with depression, with chronic pain, with long Covid, who've found something there they hadn't found anywhere else,” he says. “Cold water isn't a miracle cure, and I'm careful not to oversell it. But being outside, moving, being part of something, talking to people — that's not nothing. For some people it's a lot.”

The two teenagers from the queue, Kai and Sumaya, both 16, tell me they started coming every day in July because Kai bet Sumaya she wouldn't last a week. It's now September, and neither of them has missed a day. “We're not stopping until it closes,” says Sumaya. “Then we'll start on the river.” (Strachan, overhearing, asks them very firmly not to start on the river.)

The volunteers who never left

The restoration volunteers were supposed to go home when the builders did. Many of them didn't.

Today the lido has a volunteer roster of about 180 people, who between them give, by the society's estimate, around 12,000 hours a year. They run the reception desk on quieter sessions, look after the gardens, staff the shop that sells swimming caps and lido tote bags, guide heritage tours on open days, and sit on the society's committees. A small group of retired engineers, who call themselves “the plant room irregulars”, check the pumps and filters every morning before the staff arrive, and know the machinery, according to Strachan, “better than the people who installed it”.

Volunteering is not without tension. Paid staff and volunteers sometimes have different ideas about how things should be done, and the society has had to write policies on everything from who is allowed to hold keys to whether volunteers get free swims (they do, on a set number of sessions). In 2024, after a disagreement about café rotas spilled into a heated members' meeting, the society appointed a part-time volunteer coordinator, Imani Okwuosa, whose job is, as she puts it, “to make sure people feel thanked, and to make sure nobody is doing a sixty-hour week for free because they can't say no”.

Okwuosa says the lido is unusual in how many different kinds of people volunteer there. “You get the retired engineers and the retired teachers, sure. But you also get young people doing their Duke of Edinburgh award, people who've been out of work for a long time and want something on their CV, people who've just moved to the town and don't know anyone. I've seen friendships start in the plant room that I would never have predicted.”

One of the newest volunteers is Tomasz Wierzbicki, 34, who moved to Ashby Marsh from Poland eight years ago and works nights at a distribution centre. He volunteers on the poolside garden two mornings a week after his shift. “At work, I talk to nobody,” he says. “Here, everybody talks to me. Too much, sometimes.” He laughs. “Margaret tells me every week I am planting the lavender wrong.”

Timeline

  • 1937 — Lido opens
  • 1989 — Diving boards removed
  • 2015 — Structural survey; £1.9m repair estimate
  • 2016 — Council closes the pool
  • 2017 — Friends of Ashby Marsh Lido founded
  • 2018 — Friends become a community benefit society
  • 2019 — First community share offer
  • 2021 — “Fill the pool” crowdfunder; building work starts
  • 2023 — Lido reopens on 27 May
  • 2025 — Record season: 61,400 visits

Not everyone is a fan

It would be wrong to suggest the whole town is united behind the lido. Some residents of the streets around the pool complain about parking on summer weekends, when cars fill the creamery car park, the high street and residents' driveways. Others object to the noise of the Friday-night lido lates, which the society has since agreed to end at 9.30pm rather than 10pm, with music turned down after 9pm.

There has also been criticism of the council's role. Some argue that by handing the lido to a volunteer-led society, the council simply passed a public responsibility to the people with the most time and money to spare, and that a similar rescue would be far harder in a poorer town. “Ashby Marsh has a lot of retired professionals with time, savings and skills,” says Dr Alys Brennan, a researcher at a regional university who studies community asset transfers. “That's not a criticism of them — what they've done is remarkable. But we shouldn't pretend it's a model every town can follow. If a community has to raise a million and a half pounds to keep its pool, the places that can't will lose theirs.”

Councillor Hume, now the council's deputy leader, accepts some of this. “It's not how I'd want to fund public services in an ideal world,” she says. “But we don't live in an ideal world, and the alternative was a fenced-off hole in the ground. I'd rather have the lido run by the town than not have it at all.” The council now contributes a small annual grant towards the lido's school swimming programme, which it describes as “recognising the public benefit” of the pool.

The society, for its part, has tried to make sure the lido doesn't become a club for the comfortable. The concession rate, free under-fives swimming, the women-only and disability sessions, and a scheme that gives free season tickets to young carers are all, Strachan says, “non-negotiable, even in a bad year”.

The problem with September

There is one thing almost everyone at the lido would change, if they could: the season is too short.

Because the pool is unheated, it opens in late May, when the water reaches about 16 degrees, and closes in mid-September, when it drops below about 17 degrees and the mornings get dark. Hardcore cold-water swimmers would happily keep going, but the society's insurers and lifeguard guidance set limits, and the number of casual swimmers falls off sharply once the water is below 18 degrees.

A heated pool would extend the season by weeks at each end and bring in thousands more visits. But heating 1.8 million litres of water in an open-air pool is enormously expensive, and burning gas to do it would sit badly with a community that has spent years talking about the pool as a green, low-carbon place. The society looked at solar panels on the changing-room roofs, which would help in summer but do little in spring and autumn, and at an air-source heat pump, which would work but would cost an estimated £70,000 a year to run at current electricity prices.

The answer, if it works, is on the other side of the car park.

Cheese, milk and a heat exchanger

The Marsh Valley Creamery has been making cheese, butter and bottled milk on the edge of Ashby Marsh since 1952. It is the town's largest private employer, and its pasteurisation and cooling processes produce large amounts of low-grade waste heat — warm water at around 35 to 40 degrees — which is currently cooled in towers on the roof and released into the air.

In 2024, the creamery's operations director, Bryony Achterberg, a regular early-morning swimmer, wondered aloud in the lido café whether that heat could go somewhere more useful. The Friends' engineering volunteers, a retired heating engineer and a mechanical engineering lecturer from the nearby college, ran the numbers. Their conclusion, later confirmed by a specialist consultant, was that a heat exchanger at the creamery, connected to the lido's plant room by a 300-metre insulated pipe under the car park, could keep the pool at 22 to 24 degrees from April to October, at a running cost of a few thousand pounds a year for pumping.

“The creamery's heat is free, in the sense that they're currently paying to get rid of it,” says Kalsi, who stepped down as chair last year but still leads on building projects. “Their cooling towers use energy and water. If we take the heat, they save money too. It's one of those rare things where everyone wins.”

The project is not without risks. The heat supply depends on the creamery's production, which drops at weekends and during maintenance shutdowns, so the pool would need a small backup heater. The pipe has to cross land owned by three different parties. And the capital cost, estimated at £480,000, has not yet been fully raised: the society has secured £300,000 from a government decarbonisation fund and is planning a third share offer in the spring to cover the rest. If all goes to plan, construction will start after the 2026 season closes, and the first heated season will be 2027.

Back at the pool, Margaret Ennis has finished her lengths. She is standing on the terrace in a towel, looking at the steam coming off the water, and I ask her what she thinks about it being warmer.

She considers this. “I've swum in this pool at fourteen degrees,” she says. “I'm not sure it'll still be the same pool at twenty-four.” She pulls her towel tighter. “But I'll be ninety by then. I might let them have that one.”

The Friends of Ashby Marsh Lido's 2026 share offer is expected to open in March. Details will be published on the society's website. This article was amended on 7 November 2025 to correct the year of the first share offer, which was 2019, not 2018.
